notable_claims: Theft of service is considered appropriate when real money, such as CPU-based software license fees, is involved.
classification.summary: A reposted discussion regarding computer service policies at the University of Missouri-Rolla. The text specifically addresses the definition of 'theft of service' in a computing context, linking it to financial costs such as software licensing fees based on CPU usage.

notable_claims: Unauthorized use may constitute 'theft of service' on pay-for-access systems.
Theft charges are generally inappropriate for non-chargeback computing centers where no money changes hands.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan discusses whether unauthorized computer access should be legally classified as 'theft' or 'misuse of services.' He argues that theft charges are only justifiable when there is a direct monetary cost to the institution, such as pay-for-access systems or licensed software based on CPU time.
classification.title: Re: Policies of the U. of Missouri-Rolla, Computer Services

notable_claims: A federal judge ruled quiet reading of Playboy is not inherently sexual harassment
The poster suggests banning harassment is more appropriate than banning 'porn' on general academic computers
classification.summary: A federal district judge ruled that the quiet reading of Playboy magazine by a firefighter did not constitute a sexually harassing atmosphere. The poster uses this legal precedent to argue that academic computer policies should target harassment rather than banning pornography broadly.
classification.title: Firehouse Ban On Playboy Nixed

notable_claims: A federal judge ruled that quiet reading of Playboy magazine does not inherently create a sexually harassing atmosphere.
classification.summary: A federal judge overturned a ban on sexually explicit magazines at Los Angeles County fire stations. The ruling stated that the First Amendment protects the right of firefighters to read such publications provided they do not create a harassing atmosphere.
classification.title: Firehouse Ban On Playboy Nixed

notable_claims: Anonymity per se should not constitute a violation of system policy.
Anonymity used to evade accountability should be treated as an aggravating circumstance for penalty enhancement.
classification.summary: A reposted critique of a policy at McGill University regarding anonymity on computer systems. The text argues that anonymity itself should not be considered a violation, but rather an aggravating factor if used to evade accountability for other offenses.
classification.title: Re: McGill code

notable_claims: Anonymity per se should not constitute a violation of system policy.
The requirement for users to explicitly attach their names to messages is viewed as excessive.
classification.summary: Mitch Pravatiner critiques a policy from McGill Computing Facility (MCF) that requires all transmissions to be identifiable by staff and forbids masking identity. Pravatiner argues that anonymity should not be a violation in itself unless used to evade accountability for other prohibited acts. He suggests that requiring names beyond system-mandated identifiers is excessive.
classification.title: Re: McGill code

William December Starr argues that 'snitching' is a necessary form of force to stop online bullying and harassment, while Roger Bryner warns against giving centralized authorities power to punish such conspiracies.
